title: Environmental Xenobiotic Disruption of Lysosomal Membrane Integrity: Mechanisms and Consequences for Human Health
content:
Abstract
Humans are continuously exposed to lysosomotropic xenobiotics, including cationic amphiphilic drugs, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), redox-active heavy metals, and airborne particulates, through occupational, dietary, and environmental routes. Lysosomes are acidic organelles central to cellular degradation, nutrient sensing, and regulated cell death, and the stability of the lysosomal membrane is essential for cell viability, yet it is a preferential target for accumulation of these agents. This review synthesizes current understanding of the molecular mechanisms driving lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) and lysosomal membrane rupture (LMR) following xenobiotic exposure, and their downstream consequences for human tissue health. We review lysosomal injury, namely intralysosomal ion trapping, metal‑catalyzed Fenton chemistry, and lipid peroxidation, which converges to generate oxidative membrane pores linked to respiratory, hepatic, renal, and neurodegenerative toxicity in exposed populations. We also examine cellular membrane‑repair systems, particularly the Endosomal Sorting Complex Required for Transport (ESCRT)-III machinery and ER–lysosome lipid transfer pathways, that act to restore lysosomal integrity and limit tissue injury. Failure of these protective mechanisms initiates distinct regulated cell death programs, including apoptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis, that underlie chronic disease following sustained environmental exposure. Finally, we discuss the dual role of LMP in human health: both as a mediator of environmental toxicant‑induced injury and, more briefly, as an exploitable vulnerability in disease contexts such as drug-resistant cancer. By integrating findings from emerging non‑mammalian sentinel models and advanced imaging modalities, this review provides a framework for understanding how environmental lysosomal membrane dynamics translate into human health outcomes.
